newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss economy awaits spark from abroad-SNB's Meyer.
newsitem.headline: Swiss economy awaits spark from abroad-SNB's Meyer.

text.p: A resurgence of foreign demand remains the key to an upswing in the Swiss economy, Swiss National Bank Chairman Hans Meyer was quoted as saying.

He said in an interview with the Basler Zeitung that nearly two years of generous monetary policy had created good conditions for a recovery and that interest rates, inflation and exchange rates were favourable.
"I would think this would have an economic impact sooner or later. But there must also be a spark from abroad," he said.

Asked if he was confident the weaker Swiss franc would soon give the enconomy a lift, Meyer said: "One cannot speak of Swiss franc 'weakness'. This is much more a correction of the too marked strength of the franc that existed before."
He said it would be inappropriate to speak of a deliberate franc devaluation.

"We do not conduct exchange rate policy, but rather monetary policy," he said. "Of course this tends -- if neighbouring countries do not conduct an entirely different policy -- to have an impact on the exchange rate. But the exchange rate is just one element among others."

Asked if the SNB would devalue the franc to promote exports, Meyer said: "No one is talking about promoting exports via exchange rates, at least I am not. Once again clearly: Our task can only be to ensure favourable conditions for the overall economy. Human aspects are also important -- training, motivation, etc. But the momemtum must come from abroad.
"This was always the case in Switzerland. If our trading partners are not prospering, we cannot expect any upswing. This connection has been amply proven by many years of experience."
Meyer said the franc would probably resume its traditional position once the economy had become more normal.

"I see no reason why the franc should lose the position it has traditionally had. As long as we conduct solid policy -- that does not basically have to differ from the policy of comparable other countries -- the franc should remain a relatively strong currency," he said.

He said he doubted controversy over Swiss commercial links to Nazi Germany and Swiss banks' handling of Holocaust victims' accounts would shift the franc's traditional safe-haven currency role to the dollar. -- Zurich newsroom +41 1 631 7340
